rounds.diagnosis: blocks.0.ln1.weight[13] is exactly 0.000. Every other gain in that LayerNorm sits between about 0.71 and 0.88, so this one was almost certainly zeroed by the damage. With a zero gain, feature 13 never reaches the first attention layer, and pos.weight[1] has its largest value (+1.99) in that dimension. Losing it would blur which operand digit attention picks up. That fits the errors: most are off by one in the ones digit or the tens digit, which looks like dropped carries or slightly wrong digit sums.

flip.damage: embedding row of token '7' (tok.weight[7]) multiplied by -1

rounds.diagnosis: Most of the wrong answers are what you would get if an input digit 7 were read as 2: 70+26=46 (=20+26), 71+39=60 (=21+39), 78+95=123 (=28+95), 97+38=130 (=92+38), 27+25=47 (=22+25), 72+89=111, 73+99=122, 57+36=88 and 77+97=124. Answers that should contain a 7 are still written correctly (for example 35+43=77), so the output head looks fine. The fault seems to be in how token 7 is embedded on the input side (tok.weight[7]). That row holds the largest magnitudes in the embedding table (-2.516 at col 4, +2.259 at col 31, +1.803, +1.523), which fits it having been scaled up. Many fewer errors look like a 2 or 3 being misread as a nearby digit; this edit does not address those.

Most of the errors look like an input digit 7 being read as a smaller digit, usually 2. Examples: 70+26=46, 27+25=47, 63+37=95, 41+47=83 and 22+71=43. Last round I scaled the whole tok.weight[7] row by 0.6 and the score did not move at all. That fits the model's first step: pre-norm LayerNorm cancels any uniform scaling of a row, so the damage is more likely in the row's direction, meaning one or a few individual numbers. The strongest suspect is tok.weight[7][4] = -2.516. It is the smallest value in the whole embedding table, and every other digit has a small or positive value in column 4 (-1.07 to +1.44). A large negative spike in that one column could push 7's normalised embedding toward the code the model uses for a smaller digit. This is my best guess from reading the weights, not something I could test. I set the entry to 0 because I don't know its original value.

Most errors still come from an input digit 7 being read as 2 (for example 70+26=46, 30+37=63, 22+47=64, 42+27=64), and in nearly every case the 7 is in the input. Output 7s are mostly written correctly, so the fault is in how token 7 is embedded. Scaling the whole row did nothing, which fits LayerNorm cancelling a uniform scale, so the damage is to the row's direction. Setting tok.weight[7][4] from -2.516 to 0 gave a small gain. My best guess is that this entry had its sign flipped, so the original value was likely about +2.5. Zeroing it only removed the wrong signal. Restoring the positive value should put the token-7 embedding back in the right direction.

Three rounds of edits to tok.weight[7] moved the score by at most 0.3 points. LayerNorm cancels a uniform scale on that row, and its large entries are about the same size as large entries in other digit rows (row 6 col 9 = 3.02, row 5 col 17 = 2.85). So the embedding is probably not where the damage is. The wrong answers are also broader than "7 read as 2": a 7 is read as 3 in several cases (60+37=93, 47+10=53, 29+57=82), and some failures have no 7 in the input at all (35+43=77, 21+19=30). That points to one later component that pushes particular digit values wrong. The clearest outlier in the remaining weights is blocks.1.mlp.0.weight row 55. Its L2 norm is 1.41, about twice the median of 0.67 and well above the next largest (1.13). That fits a hidden neuron whose input weights were scaled up, so it fires too strongly and distorts the digit sums in the second block.

swap.damage: embedding rows of tokens '3' and '8' (tok.weight[3], tok.weight[8]) swapped

rounds.diagnosis: The embedding rows for tokens '3' and '8' have been swapped, so the model reads every input 3 as an 8 and every 8 as a 3. The model's arithmetic is otherwise correct. Checking against the wrong answers: 35+43 gives 133, which equals 85+48. 82+41 gives 73, which equals 32+41. 43+49 gives 97, which equals 48+49. 12+80 gives 42, which equals 12+30. 80+98 gives 123, which equals 30+93. The output digits match these swapped sums, so the output head is not damaged.

flip#2.damage: embedding row of token '7' (tok.weight[7]) multiplied by -1

rounds.diagnosis: Most of the wrong answers have a 7 in one of the operands, and the model treats that 7 as roughly a 2 (sometimes a 3), whether it is in the tens or the units place. For example, 70+26 gives 46, 21+75 gives 46, 22+47 gives 64, 31+71 gives 52 and 30+79 gives 59. A consistent shift of 5 (7→2) is what you would expect if the 7 embedding had been negated: if the digit embeddings encode digits periodically (mod 10), flipping the sign acts like adding 5 to the digit. I can't test this here, so it's a hypothesis. tok.weight[7] also has unusually large values (-2.5, +2.3), which suggests that row was the one damaged.

flip#3.damage: embedding row of token '7' (tok.weight[7]) multiplied by -1

rounds.diagnosis: Nearly every wrong answer comes out as if the digit 7 had been read as a 2, and this happens wherever the 7 sits. Examples: 70+26 gives 46 (=20+26), 78+95 gives 123 (=28+95), 27+25 gives 47 (=22+25), 57+36 gives 88 (=52+36) and 63+37 gives 95 (=63+32). Other digits are read correctly, so the damage is most likely in the input embedding for token 7 (tok.weight[7]). My best guess is that this row's sign was flipped. That is unconfirmed: tok.weight[7] does not look like a copy of row 2.
